🐛 Bug
torch.optim.lr_scheduler.SequentialLR inherits the _LRScheduler class but it doesn't have an optimizer attribute. It might not be a bug, but it does bring inconvenience when users try to access that attribute.
For example, when I use Pytorch Lightning, I specified this SequentialLR inside the configure_optimizer() function of the lightning module. At the time when the training is launched, there's a sanity check to make sure the optimizers and the lr schedulers are matching.
Given that SequentialLR.optimizer doesn't exist, I'm getting the following attribute error:
AttributeError: 'SequentialLR' object has no attribute 'optimizer'

which is annoying.
Since SequentialLR already guarantee that all schedulers belong to the same optimizer, why not assign it the optimizer attribute? The fix would be very easy, just add one more line in the constructor:
self.optimizer = optimizer

import torch
model = torch.nn.Linear(2,2)

lr_scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.SequentialLR(optim, [torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ConstantLR(optim), torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optim, step_size=10)], [1])

lr_scheduler.optimizer

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature

Ask for DDP wrapper of nn.Module supports a new flag that allow different batch size across processes. So that when invoking the loss.backward(), DDP won't automatically do sum(grad)/num_replicas.
This is kind of duplicated to #31553 . But I think my case is more concrete.
Motivation

Basically, there're two potential situations:

The performance across GPUs is different (e.g. Tesla V100 vs. GTX 1080Ti). We may want the GPU with better perf being fed with larger batch size.
Dealing with sequence problem of variable length data. To arranging variable-length data into batch, commonly we add paddings to align them to the max length. However, for DDP, this can be optimized via balancing the data on GPUs. This figure might help better explain the difference of the native ( DistributedSampler) and a optimized sampler


Pitch

Alternatives

Currently, we can do that in a hack way.
# on each process. 
# get batch size on local process 
local_batch_size = ...
# suppose the loss is reduce by 'mean', calculate the sum of loss on local process
local_loss_sum = loss.detach() * local_batch_size
# local_batch_size is reduced to global batch size
dist.all_reduce(local_batch_size)
global_batch_size = local_batch_size
# modify the loss in-place
loss.data = local_loss_sum * world_size / global_batch_size
loss.backward()
With this normalized loss, now in the loss.backward(), the DDP is actually doing
sum(local_grad_sum * world_size / global_batch_size)/world_size
=global_grad_sum / global_batch_size

And it's the correct way of back-propagation with different batch size across GPUs.

Offloading data to CPU can reduce GPU memory footprint, allowing a larger model to be trained. 🚀 Feature
Add an option to the variants of Adam in pytorch which allows you to only apply the bias correction term to the denominator (the variance estimate on the gradient: v_t). (For example, optionally set step_size = lr vs dividing by bias_correction1 eg on this line)
Motivation
In the Adam/AdamW/etc optimizer, a bias correction term of (1-B_{1,2}^t) is applied to both m (the first-moment estimate of the gradient) and v (the second moment estimate of the gradient). This inflates these terms early in training since it is a division by a number in (0, 1). While inflating the early estimate of variance away from zero is a great idea, since it's the denominator in the gradient update, inflating the numerator is not well justified, in my opinion. This can result in some steps that are even larger than the requested learning rate early in training. I discuss these issues in AdamD: Improved bias-correction in Adam.
This following figure shows the effect of Adam's current bias-correction strategy on the learning rate early in training, vs my proposed alternative:

Pitch
I would be happy to implement this. It could be an option added to all of the Adam/AdamW/etc optimizers that is False by default to prevent any backwards compatibility issues, but allows users to experiment with this alternative approach.
Alternatives

An option to exclude the bias correction term completely may be reasonable, but since v_t is initialized to zero this could be less stable than simply only bias correcting v_t as proposed.
A new optimizer class, AdamD. I don't love this option because it would be really easy to add this as a flag to existing Adam variant optimizers, and the concept should apply to all of them equally.

Additional context

While the vast majority of PyTorch functions and classes can be wrapped and unwrapped without modifying behavior (as far as I can tell), __getitem__ is unable to support tensor indexing when wrapped. This issue persists even after unwrapping back to the original function.
While this is not a typical PyTorch use case, issues such as this make monkey-patching, API wrapping, and non-standard dynamic customizations a challenge.
I realize flagging this as a bug might be stretch, but I presume ideally the code below should run without error. If you deem that this does not constitute a bug or desired PyTorch behavior, then I will happily close the issue.
To Reproduce
import torch

def wrap(fn):

    def new_fn(*a, **kw):
        return fn(*a, **kw)

    new_fn.inner_fn = fn

    return new_fn


x = torch.ones((2,))

# before wrap
x[0]  # works
x[0:1]  # works
x[torch.tensor([0, 1])]  # works

# wrap
torch.Tensor.__getitem__ = wrap(torch.Tensor.__getitem__)

# after wrap
x[0]  # works
x[0:1]  # works
x[torch.tensor([0, 1])]  # IndexError: too many indices for tensor of dimension 1

# unwrap
torch.Tensor.__getitem__ = torch.Tensor.__getitem__.inner_fn

# after unwrap
x[0]  # works

🚀 Feature
We need _full_param_padded attribute on sharded parameter to be able to rematerialize the full parameter before forward/backward of the layer.
In _lazy_init, when we create this, we allocate the entire large tensor (via torch.zeros) and then immediately free its storage. The tensor retains properties such as size, device, and dtype which is what's needed to rematerialize it appropriately as needed.
It seems we can avoid this entire allocation, which currently occurs every iteration, if we just record the size, device, dtype, instead of create + deallocate the tensor.
Possibly some sort of meta tensor/meta device API, similar to #66317 (but that is for nn.Modules) can be used when that API is available. Alternatively today seems that it can just be done via a simple dataclass.
Note that this won't actually decrease peak memory usage because we still need to rematerialize the full parameter eventually. But it could be a perf optimization especially if tensor is very large because this happens every iteration today.

In FSDP we run all_gather on separate stream, thus we need to wait for the current stream corresponding to previous optimizer step to ensure parameters are up to date.

Sometimes, this is intentional, but often times, I suspect it is accidental or due to oversight/unawareness. These test cases miss out on the customizations we place in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/testing/_internal/common_utils.py#L1307, which include:

Not enjoying the functionality of pre-written wrappers
The CI not being able to check and skip if they are a slow test
The CI not being able to check and skip if they are disabled

To enforce this, we can check in run_tests() if the test is a vanilla unittest.TestCase  and error when that is the case. This would capture the case where the test writer is trying to use all the features in common_utils.py but neglected to extend the right TestCase. This would also allow test classes that intend to use the vanilla TestCase to do so without being yelled at.

🐛 Bug
When symbolic script creates a DifferentiableGraph where a variable is used inside the graph, and also is output of the graph and used in subsequent operations, the contribution from subsequent operations is not added to the gradient.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Enable layer_norm in symbolic script, recompile pytorch:

diff --git a/torch/csrc/jit/runtime/symbolic_script.cpp b/torch/csrc/jit/runtime/symbolic_script.cpp
index 8a0266e7db..b0fbe60ba6 100644
--- a/torch/csrc/jit/runtime/symbolic_script.cpp
+++ b/torch/csrc/jit/runtime/symbolic_script.cpp
@@ -1141,7 +1141,7 @@ const std::vector<std::string> functions = {
 
             return output, backward
 
-        def layer_norm_disabled(input : Tensor,
+        def layer_norm(input : Tensor,
                        normalized_shape : List[int],


Run the following script. The output will be something like

eager model
Starting iterations 
=== iteration: 0, loss: 4.378854274749756 ===
backward
end backward
=== iteration: 1, loss: 2.726267099380493 ===
backward
end backward
script model
Starting iterations 
=== iteration: 0, loss: 4.378854274749756 ===
backward
end backward
=== iteration: 1, loss: 10.749004364013672 ===
backward
end backward

Note how even though model is deterministic, the loss of the second iteration is very different in the scripted mode than in the eager mode. Also note that to get these results you need to disable profiling executor, otherwise it doesn't create DifferentiableSubgraph. You can set debug=True in the last line to get more info.
Expected behavior
Symbolic script should produce correct gradients
Environment
Fresh master build
Additional Context
The problem is with the DifferentiableGraph created by symbolic_script (run with debug=True to get a print of DifferentiableGraph). The relevant part of the model is as follows:
        norm = self.layer_norm(dense_out)
        split_sum = self.linear_split_1(norm) #* 2 + 1
        prod = self.linear(split_sum) * norm #* 2 + 1
        interaction = torch.sum(torch.stack([norm, prod], dim=0), dim=0)

Note how norm, which is layer_norm output, participates in linear_split_1 (where it is split into 3 parts and other things are done to it), prod, where split_sum is multiplied by norm again, and interaction. That means that dY for layer_norm should have contributions from all these 3 functions.
DifferentialGraph0 is as follows:
with prim::DifferentiableGraph_0 = graph(%weight.28 : Float(*, requires_grad=0, device=cpu),
      %bias.28 : Float(*, requires_grad=0, device=cpu),
      %input.6 : Float(*, *, requires_grad=0, device=cpu),
      %weight.30 : Float(*, *, requires_grad=0, device=cpu),
      %bias.30 : Float(*, requires_grad=0, device=cpu)):
  %1 : int[] = prim::Constant[value=[85, 85, 86]]()
  %8 : float = prim::Constant[value=1.0000000000000001e-05]()
  %5 : int[] = prim::Constant[value=[256]]()
  %69 : int = prim::Constant[value=1]() # <string>:76:118
  %16 : Tensor(requires_grad=0) = aten::linear(%input.6, %weight.30, %bias.30), scope: __module.dense_arch # /data/users/ngimel/pytorch/torch/nn/functional.py:1896:0
  %input.9 : Tensor(requires_grad=0) = aten::relu(%16) # /data/users/ngimel/pytorch/../playground/autodiff_layer_norm.py:108:0
  %output.1 : Tensor(requires_grad=0), %mean.4 : Tensor, %rstd.4 : Tensor = aten::native_layer_norm(%input.9, %5, %weight.28, %bias.28, %8) # <string>:33:33
  %22 : Tensor[] = aten::split_with_sizes(%output.1, %1, %69) # <string>:128:19
  return (%22, %output.1, %input.9, %mean.4, %rstd.4)

It returns raw output of layer_norm as output.1, and it seems that contributions from prod and interaction should flow to gradOutput of output.1 and then be added to the gradInput computed by split_with_sizes backward (which is cat) before being passed to layer_norm_backward. Yet that's not what's happening in script, I'm printing means of cat inputs and layer_norm_backward dY:
0 tensor mean -0.000689346 size [32, 85] stride [85, 1]
1 tensor mean 0.00053283 size [32, 85] stride [85, 1]
2 tensor mean 0.000168846 size [32, 86] stride [86, 1]
cat serial result 4.75354e-06 [32, 256][256, 1]
layer norm dY 4.75354e-06 input 0.139588 weight 1

cat output directly flows to layer_norm_backward as dY!
In non-scripted mode, that's not the case, and layer_norm dY is different from cat output:
0 tensor mean -0.000689346 size [32, 85] stride [85, 1]
1 tensor mean 0.00053283 size [32, 85] stride [85, 1]
2 tensor mean 0.000168846 size [32, 86] stride [86, 1]
cat serial result 4.75351e-06 [32, 256][256, 1]
layer norm dY 0.000410447 input 0.139588 weight 1

Even though this particular bug is triggered only with legacy executor, it's a genuine bug in autodiff construction, and if profiling executor was able to construct this DifferentiableGraph, it would hit the same.
